description.value: A high, short-burst speech pitched to cut the shelf wind, delivered in the gaps between gusts so that a sentence takes as long as the weather allows. Repetition is the grammar rather than a stylistic habit: said once a thing is a proposal, said twice it is an assertion of fact, and said three times it is a call for a wall to be worked at once. It carries positions, instructions and holdings very well and cannot carry a conditional at all, so anything hypothetical is put in tail movement instead and is lost from an audio recording entirely. Fieldworkers hear the doubled forms as anger for about a season, and the early transcripts accordingly record a placid exchange about mud depth as a sustained quarrel.

sampleGloss.value: meirau meirau, leiwa nauoti - wall wall, water go-out-now - the wall is holding; I am telling you this, not asking you.

note.value: Recorded during elicitation and kept as the reference sample for this system.
